planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Goodland is extremely cold-hardy and bred for prairie climates, zone 3a and up.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Goodland was selected at Morden Research Station in Manitoba in 1925 from a Patten Greening seedling and introduced in 1955, bred specifically to survive brutal prairie winters down to zone 3a. Fruit is medium-sized, light green washed with red, with creamy, fine-textured flesh good for both fresh eating and cooking, and keeps in storage for roughly 20 weeks. It remains a standard recommendation for cold-climate orchards across the northern Great Plains and Canadian prairies where many other apple cultivars simply cannot survive the winter.
sources: University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Battleford is one of the hardiest apples available, suited to zone 2a prairie winters.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Battleford was bred by amateur breeder Murray Sommerville in North Battleford, Saskatchewan and introduced by Boughen Nursery in 1934. It produces large golden-yellow fruit blushed with red, crisp and mildly tart, on a tree hardy to zone 2a and showing moderate resistance to fire blight. This is a true prairie workhorse apple, grown where winter cold rules out most other cultivars, and remains a staple recommendation for Canadian prairie home orchards.
sources: University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Parkland is self-fertile but bears biennially, so expect a lighter crop every other year.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Parkland was bred at Morden Research Station in Manitoba in 1979 from a cross of Melba and Rescue, hardy to zone 2 and tolerant of temperatures approaching -46°C. It bears small, firm, sweet-tart apples that keep about 8 weeks and is precocious but tends toward biennial bearing. Parkland became the leading commercial apple cultivar in Alaska thanks to its extreme cold hardiness, and it remains a reliable choice anywhere winter survival matters more than fruit size.
sources: University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator nearby; Heyer 12 needs cross-pollination to fruit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator, since Heyer 12 requires cross-pollination to set fruit. Selected by amateur breeder Adolph Heyer of Neville, Saskatchewan from Russian apple seed obtained from fellow breeder A.P. Stevenson of Morden, Manitoba, and introduced in 1940, it is extremely hardy to zone 1-2 and notably resistant to fire blight. The medium yellow-green fruit is quite tart and best suited to cooking rather than fresh eating, making it a workhorse culinary apple for the coldest prairie orchards where few other cultivars survive at all.
sources: University of Saskatchewan fruit breeding program

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; September Ruby ripens early and stores several months in a cool cellar.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; September Ruby is a Rescue x Haralson cross released in 1986 by the Prairie Fruit Breeding Cooperative working out of Morden, Manitoba and Beaverlodge, Alberta. It bears medium, round-oblate fruit colored light green striped and blushed with bright, dark red over crisp, moderately acid flesh, maturing in early-to-mid September and keeping about 16 weeks in storage. It is a solid dual-purpose apple for cold-climate orchards, bred specifically for zone 2a hardiness on the Canadian prairies.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Hibernal is vigorous and prolific, among the hardiest of the old Russian apple cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Hibernal was imported from Russia to North America around 1870 as part of settler-era efforts to find apples that could survive brutal continental winters, and is considered among the hardiest of the old Russian apple race. The vigorous, prolific tree shows good resistance to scab, fire blight, and rust, and was historically valued both for its own culinary fruit, which keeps into January, and as exceptionally hardy framework or rootstock material for grafting less cold-tolerant varieties. It remains a useful heritage choice for cold-climate orchards prioritizing toughness over fresh-eating quality.
sources: Montana State University Western Agricultural Research Center heritage orchard records

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Charlamoff ripens in late August and is best used fresh from the tree for cooking rather than long storage.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Charlamoff is a Russian Duchess-type apple imported by J.L. Budd for Iowa Agricultural College in the late 1800s and was ranked among the hardiest cultivars by the Minnesota State Horticultural Society in its era. It ripens in late August, with lavender-pink striped skin over white flesh that stains red near the surface, firm, crisp, and juicy, best suited to cooking rather than long-term storage. As a 19th-century Russian heirloom bred for extreme cold tolerance, it remains a solid choice for northern heritage orchards.
sources: South Dakota State University Open Prairie historical bulletin

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Red Astrachan is an early-season apple best used quickly for cooking or cider rather than stored.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Red Astrachan is an ancient Russian apple cultivar documented in Sweden by 1780 and brought to the United States by 1835, where it also acquired the regional nickname 'Abe Lincoln' through its association with Lincoln's boyhood Illinois homestead. It ripens early in the season with juicy, tart, somewhat mealy flesh under brightly striped red skin, best used quickly for cooking, cider, or drying rather than fresh eating or long storage. As one of the oldest documented apple cultivars still in cultivation, it holds genuine historical as well as culinary interest for a heritage orchard.
sources: National Park Service heritage orchard records

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Durondeau is partially self-fertile but crops more heavily with a second pear cultivar nearby.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Durondeau was raised near Tournai, Belgium around 1811 by Charles Louis Durondeau and is regarded as Belgium's unofficial national pear, sometimes called 'la reine des poires' (the queen of pears). It bears large, conical, calabasse-shaped fruit with golden, often red-flushed, russeted skin over white, melting, sweet-tart flesh. The tree is partially self-fertile and a heavy, regular cropper, making it a reliable choice for a heritage pear orchard alongside more commonly grown dessert pears.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Governor Wood is self-fertile and ripens early, ahead of most other sweet cherries.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Governor Wood is an American duke-type sweet cherry introduced in 1842, bearing golden-yellow skin blushed with red over firm, tender, richly flavored flesh that resists cracking better than many sweet cherries. It is self-fertile, sweeter than the familiar pie cherry Montmorency, and ripens early with a heavy crop, making it a good heritage choice for home orchards that want an early-season sweet cherry without needing a second pollinator tree.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator; Early Rivers is one of the earliest-ripening sweet cherries available.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator; Early Rivers was bred by Thomas Rivers at his Sawbridgeworth, Hertfordshire nursery between 1869 and 1872 from an Early Purple Gean seedling, and won an RHS First Class Certificate in 1872. It produces large, near-black, heart-shaped fruit with very good sweet flavor in late June, among the earliest-ripening sweet cherries, and became the standard early cherry grown commercially in Kent, England. It remains a strong choice for gardeners wanting cherries ahead of the main summer season.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator; Windsor is a productive, historically important Canadian sweet cherry.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator; Windsor originated on James Dougall's farm in Windsor, Ontario and was introduced in 1871, going on to become Ontario's dominant commercial sweet cherry for decades before later cultivars like Hedelfingen and Vic took over. It bears small, light-colored, firm fruit on a productive tree, and has been used as a parent in Canadian sweet cherry breeding programs since 1917. It remains a worthwhile heritage cultivar for a home orchard with Canadian or Great Lakes roots.
sources: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs cherry cultivar guide

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator; Merton Bigarreau is not self-fertile and ripens late, in late July.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun alongside a compatible pollinator, since Merton Bigarreau is not self-fertile. Bred in 1924 at the John Innes Horticultural Institution in England from a cross of Knight's Early Black and Napoleon Bigarreau, it is part of the Institution's series of Merton cherry introductions. The vigorous, heavy-cropping tree bears dark red-black, firm, richly flavored fruit in late July, later in the season than most other sweet cherries in this batch, extending the home-orchard sweet cherry harvest window.
